films.title: A light bulb at Dendera and a rocket at Palenque? Read the captions
films.hook: A light bulb and a rocket?
films.caption:
In a crypt at Dendera, in Egypt, a carving looks like a giant bulb, but its hieroglyphs name a snake god rising from a lotus, and give its material: gold. At Palenque, in Mexico, the lid seen as a rocket names King Pakal, who died in 683, and shows the Maya World Tree. Experts still debate whether the king is falling into the underworld or rising reborn.

Do the Dendera bulb carving and Pakal's tomb lid show an electric lamp and a rocket? Verdict: Ruled out.

films.title: Is Atlantis under the Atlantic? What the sea floor and Spartel Bank show
films.caption:
In 1882, Ignatius Donnelly read the great ridge down the Atlantic as the drowned spine of Atlantis, not a silly guess then. Sound maps and drilling show the ridge is where new sea floor is born, and light continental rock does not sink. Spartel Bank, a small drowned island outside the Strait of Gibraltar, would probably have held simple fishermen, not an empire.

Could a sunken continent, Atlantis, lie on the Atlantic floor beyond Gibraltar? Verdict: Ruled out.

films.title: Were the Nazca lines runways? How people drew giant figures in the desert
films.caption:
The Nazca figures in southern Peru were made by moving dark, rust-coated stones aside to show the pale ground beneath, which is far too soft for a runway. In 1982, Joe Nickell and five relatives used stakes and cord to plot a condor a hundred and thirty-four metres long in a Kentucky field, and from the air it matched. What the giant lines were for is still argued.

Were some of the Nazca lines in Peru made as runways for visitors from the sky? Verdict: Ruled out.

films.title: The Eye of the Sahara, Bimini and Santorini: was any of them Atlantis?
films.caption:
The Eye of the Sahara, rings of rock forty kilometres across, is eight times too big and far from the sea; the squared stones off Bimini are beachrock, with shells about three and a half thousand years old. Thera, today's Santorini, erupted around 1600 BCE, but Plato puts Atlantis beyond the Pillars of Heracles. Thera was a real catastrophe, and perhaps a distant memory.

Was Plato's Atlantis the Eye of the Sahara, the stones off Bimini, or the island of Thera? Verdict: Ruled out.

films.title: Klerksdorp spheres and the Baghdad battery: lost technology, weighed
films.caption:
The grooved Klerksdorp spheres from South African mines are concretions, geologists say, and a steel blade scratches them. The clay jar found near Baghdad in 1936 holds a copper tube and an iron rod, and replicas filled with lemon juice give about half a volt. But no wires were found with it, and similar jars held rolls of papyrus: perhaps a holder for a blessing.

Was the clay jar found near Baghdad in 1936 a working battery in its own time? Verdict: Awaiting evidence.

films.title: Helike: the real city of Poseidon that sank in one night in Plato's lifetime
films.hook: Did a real city sink in a night?
films.caption:
In the winter of 373 BCE, an earthquake by night and then the sea took Helike, a city famous for its temple of Poseidon, less than a hundred and fifty kilometres from Athens. Ninety-nine boreholes later found its ruins some three metres down, under what is dry land today. About a dozen years later, Plato wrote Atlantis; whether Helike shaped it, we can't know.

Did Helike, a real city of Poseidon, sink into the sea in a single night in Plato's lifetime? Verdict: Established.

films.caption:
At Baalbek in Lebanon, a Roman temple to Jupiter sits on a platform holding three limestone blocks about nineteen metres long, and the writer Graham Hancock fairly asks if they are older than Rome. The giant platform wraps around an older, smaller one, and quarry pottery dates to early Roman times. The test is a sealed layer under the trilithon.

Are the giant lower courses at Baalbek older than the Roman temple built on top of them? Verdict: Awaiting evidence.

films.title: How hunters carved Göbekli Tepe's stone giants without metal
films.caption:
On a ridge in southeast Turkey, round enclosures hold T-shaped stone pillars with carved arms, hands and belts: giants in stone. They were cut in the quarry next door with flint picks, by people who ate gazelle and wild cattle: animals hunted, not herded. The textbooks said farming first, then monuments; here the giants came first.

Did people raise Göbekli Tepe's stone giants without metal, pottery or farm animals? Verdict: Established.

films.title: How do you move a 1,000-tonne stone? Sledges, wet sand, capstans and rope
films.caption:
The enemy is friction, not weight: an Egyptian tomb scene shows a statue of about sixty tonnes on a sledge as a man pours water on the sand, and in 2014 physicists found the right amount of water cuts the pull by about half. In 1770, about four hundred people in Russia hauled a granite boulder of more than a thousand tonnes. How Baalbek's giants were raised is still unknown.

Did moving stones of a thousand tonnes need a lost high technology? Verdict: Ruled out.

films.title: Was Göbekli Tepe buried on purpose, or did the hillside slide in?
films.hook: Buried by hand, or by the hill?
films.caption:
Rubble moves, so to date Göbekli Tepe the excavators also dated plaster put on its walls while the buildings stood. For about twenty years the story was that people buried the enclosures on purpose. In 2020 the excavators argued most of the fill slid in from the slopes, but at sister site Karahan Tepe, fill capped with big flat stones looks deliberate.

Were Göbekli Tepe's enclosures buried on purpose, or did rubble slide in from the slopes above? Verdict: Open question.

films.title: Puma Punku in 15,000 BCE? What radiocarbon and metal cramps say
films.caption:
High in the Andes of Bolivia, Puma Punku's andesite blocks are cut with crisp inside corners. Arthur Posnansky dated the city to about fifteen thousand BCE from where its walls point at the sky, but radiocarbon from the platform's lowest fill gives about AD 536 to 600, and its metal cramps match Tiwanaku's own era. The tools that cut those corners are still unknown.

Was the Puma Punku platform in Bolivia built around fifteen thousand BCE? Verdict: Ruled out.

films.hook: A lost world behind the giants?

The writer Graham Hancock argues that something as ambitious as Göbekli Tepe is no first attempt, and that survivors of a lost Ice Age civilisation may have taught local hunters. Such visitors should leave something with no local roots. So far the dig shows local stone, local tools, homes, cisterns and about a dozen sister sites, but nothing yet from outside.

Did survivors of a lost Ice Age civilisation pass their knowledge to Göbekli Tepe's builders? Verdict: Awaiting evidence.

films.caption:
Above Cusco in Peru, Sacsayhuamán's stones of well over a hundred tonnes fit so tightly that a knife blade won't slide between them, and some writers say older builders laid them. Chroniclers writing within a generation describe an Inca work, and Jean-Pierre Protzen came close to the fit with hammerstones. People lived there from about 900 CE, but no older wall has been dated.

Were the giant lower stones of Sacsayhuamán, above Cusco, laid by builders older than the Incas? Verdict: Awaiting evidence.

films.hook: A comet on the Vulture Stone?
films.caption:
In 2017, the engineer Martin Sweatman read Göbekli Tepe's Vulture Stone as a star map, dated close to a proposed comet strike at the start of the Younger Dryas. The excavators replied that their oldest date for its enclosure is seven hundred to a thousand years younger, and that star matching is flexible. So far, the stars and the stone disagree by centuries.

Does the Vulture Stone at Göbekli Tepe record a comet strike at the start of the Younger Dryas? Verdict: Awaiting evidence.

films.caption:
Gunung Padang crowns a hill in West Java: five stone terraces, climbing like giant steps. Under the retaining walls, archaeologists found charcoal from fires lit before the walls went up, dating the terraces to about two thousand years ago, built over several generations. Its stone beams came not from a distant quarry but out of the hill itself.

Did people build Gunung Padang's stone terraces about two thousand years ago? Verdict: Established.

films.title: Derinkuyu: a city cut into soft volcanic rock and built for hiding
films.caption:
Cappadocia's tuff, a soft stone of volcanic ash, can be cut with hand tools and keeps rooms at a steady temperature. At Derinkuyu, reports count up to eighteen levels, with stables, wine presses, a church and more than fifty air shafts. Stone wheels up to almost two metres across rolled shut from inside, sealing each level on its own: a city built for hiding.

Was Derinkuyu, sealed by rolling stone doors, a refuge built for people to hide in? Verdict: Established.

films.title: How cooling lava made Gunung Padang's straight-edged stone columns
films.caption:
Gunung Padang's long stone beams, five or six sided with edges that look cut, are columnar andesite: lava that shrank and cracked into columns as it cooled, as at the Giant's Causeway. Indonesian volcanologists read the hill as the neck of an ancient volcano, its columns formed right where they lie. Nature made the bricks; the question is who stacked them, and when.

Were Gunung Padang's straight-edged stone beams shaped by cooling lava, not cut by people? Verdict: Established.

films.title: Beyond Derinkuyu: Kaymakli, Ozkonak and the city found under Nevsehir
films.caption:
Derinkuyu is not alone: Kaymakli lies about ten kilometres north, draining irrigation water revealed Ozkonak in 1972, and surveyors list more than two hundred underground shelters. Under Nevsehir, where families long used the old passages as cellars, finds so far run from about the sixth century to today. Scans there hinted at a city perhaps a third bigger than Derinkuyu.

Were Cappadocia's underground cities used as shelters and cellars into the twentieth century? Verdict: Established.

films.title: Is there an Ice Age pyramid inside Gunung Padang? The team's case
films.hook: A pyramid from the Ice Age?
films.caption:
From 2011, a team led by the geologist Danny Hilman Natawidjaja probed Gunung Padang with radar, electric current and seven drill cores. They read buried layers of columns laid like bricks, a possible chamber where drilling water vanished, and soil dated deep into the Ice Age. If they are right, it is the oldest great building on Earth, by far.

Do the scans, cores and soil dates show a pyramid built inside Gunung Padang in the Ice Age? Verdict: Awaiting evidence.

The writer Graham Hancock asks whether Cappadocia's underground cities began as shelters from the Ice Age cold of nearly thirteen thousand years ago. He has a point: nobody has ever dated the digging itself, and an empty carved room holds nothing to radiocarbon date. And each enlargement scraped older surfaces away, so the deepest room could be very old, or fairly new.

films.title: Why a journal retracted the Gunung Padang Ice Age pyramid paper
films.caption:
The 2023 Gunung Padang pyramid paper dated soil packed between the stones, not charcoal from a hearth, a bone or a tool. Radiocarbon dates when that carbon stopped being alive, not when a stone was laid on top. The journal retracted it in March 2024; the authors say the soil came from built layers, but a date for soil is not a date for a pyramid.

films.hook: Who hid below, and from whom?
films.caption:
In Cappadocia's underground cities, what can be dated is what people left: crosses, churches and Byzantine pottery. From the six hundreds the region was a raided Byzantine frontier, and families led their animals below and rolled the stones shut. Most specialists date the great cities to those centuries, but earlier starts, by Phrygians or Hittites, stay open.

films.hook: Did the Ice Age come back?
films.caption:
About 14,700 years ago, central Greenland warmed by about fourteen degrees, then the north slid back towards Ice Age cold: the Younger Dryas. Yearly bands in Greenland ice put it from about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago, while mud layers in a German crater lake start it more than a century and a half later. The cold itself is not in doubt; what pulled the trigger is.

Did the north slide back towards Ice Age cold about 12,900 years ago? Verdict: Established.

films.title: The Voynich manuscript's calfskin dates to between about 1404 and 1438
films.hook: How old is the unreadable book?
films.caption:
In 1912, the book dealer Wilfrid Voynich bought a batch of old manuscripts near Rome, and inside one lay a letter written in Prague in about 1665. Some suspected Voynich of forging it, but in 2009 radiocarbon dating of its calfskin gave between about 1404 and 1438, and its paints are pigments of the age. Its plants, stars and bathing women still wait for a reader.

Is the Voynich manuscript a real book from the early 1400s rather than a modern fake? Verdict: Established.

films.title: Did a comet explode over North America 12,900 years ago? The case for it
films.hook: Did a comet bring the cold?
films.caption:
In 2007, a team proposed that a comet exploded over North America about 12,900 years ago and tipped the climate into cold. They reported melted beads, soot and nanodiamonds at the base of a dark layer, the black mat, and Greenland ice shows a platinum spike near the cold's start. One sudden cause would link the cold, the lost giant animals and the end of Clovis tools.

Did a comet explode over North America about 12,900 years ago and tip the climate into cold? Verdict: Awaiting evidence.

films.title: Does the Voynich text behave like a real language? What the counts show
films.hook: Does it count as a language?
films.caption:
You can't read the Voynich manuscript, but you can count it. Its words follow the same staircase of frequencies as real languages, crowd by topic like real words, and split into two dialects written by five scribes. Yet its next letter is far easier to guess, matching none of nearly three hundred languages: word by word a language, letter by letter like none we know.

Do the statistics of the Voynich text point to a real language hidden in its pages? Verdict: Open question.

films.title: Are the Carolina Bays craters from a comet blast? Dating the buried sand
films.caption:
No crater of the right age has been found for the Younger Dryas comet, though an airburst can leave none. Other teams failed to repeat several clues and found the same markers in black mats of many different ages; the comet team disputes their methods. The Carolina Bays were proposed as its craters, but buried sand dates their rims from 109,000 down to 2,000 years old.

Are the Carolina Bays, half a million oval hollows in the eastern United States, a comet's craters? Verdict: Ruled out.

films.title: A century of claimed Voynich solutions, and the test every one has failed
films.caption:
In 1921 a professor read a hidden message in tiny strokes inside the letters; in 1931 they turned out to be cracks where the ink had dried. Wartime codebreakers under William Friedman never cracked the Voynich manuscript, and readings in Hebrew, Latin and Turkish keep coming. A real reading must follow fixed rules, work on every page, and give a stranger the same text.

Has any claimed solution of the last century actually read the Voynich manuscript? Verdict: Ruled out.

films.title: Did a meltwater flood slow the Atlantic and bring back the cold?
films.caption:
Most specialists blame the Younger Dryas cold on meltwater, floating on the Atlantic like a lid and slowing its conveyor of warmth. Arctic seabed cores show a flood down Canada's Mackenzie River that began, within the clocks' margins, just as the cold did. A new reading, still being tested, puts the Greenland platinum spike about forty-five years after the cooling began.

Did a flood of meltwater slow the Atlantic's conveyor belt and trigger the Younger Dryas cold? Verdict: Open question.

films.title: Is the Voynich manuscript beautiful nonsense, or a cipher?
films.caption:
In 2004 Gordon Rugg showed that a card with windows, slid over a table of meaningless syllables, makes text very like the Voynich manuscript's. In 2022, volunteers' fake text came out predictable and repetitive too, but so does text from some ciphers, and a 2025 cipher built from dice and playing cards mimics it as well. Nonsense can look like this, and so can a cipher.

Could the Voynich text be meaningless writing, made by hand to look like a language? Verdict: Open question.

films.title: Did a comet blast push Abu Hureyra's villagers into farming?
films.hook: A comet and the first farmers?
films.caption:
At Abu Hureyra in Syria, glass the comet team links to a blast is still argued over: another team traced similar droplets to burning mud-brick houses. As the cold set in, the villagers may have begun to cultivate wild rye, some of the first farming on Earth, though others read the seeds differently. The cold mattered either way; who started it is a separate question.

Did a comet blast melt the glass at Abu Hureyra and push its survivors to take up farming? Verdict: Awaiting evidence.

films.title: The gold Schliemann named Priam's treasure: about a thousand years too early
films.caption:
In 1868 Frank Calvert showed Heinrich Schliemann a mound called Hisarlik, in northwest Turkey, and from 1871 Schliemann drove a vast trench through it. In 1873 he found gold he named the treasure of Priam, but it came from Troy Two, more than a thousand years older than any date for the war. On the way down, his trench cut away much of the very layers he was looking for.

Was the gold Schliemann found at Troy in 1873 the treasure of Priam, Troy's king in the Iliad? Verdict: Ruled out.

films.title: Who were the Sea Peoples? Egypt's temple carvings and the DNA of Ashkelon
films.caption:
Around 1177 BCE, Ramesses the Third carved his battle with invaders from land and sea on his temple, Medinet Habu: the winner's version. Egypt's texts name nine of these peoples, and one, the Peleset, is usually matched with the Philistines. In 2019, DNA from infants at Ashkelon pointed to newcomers, probably from southern Europe: raiders, but also families who stayed.

Were the Sea Peoples real raiders and migrants who brought destruction? Verdict: Established.

films.title: Walls up to five metres thick: Troy Six and the quarrel over its lower town
films.caption:
Wilhelm Doerpfeld uncovered the walls of Troy Six, stone up to five metres thick. From 1988, Manfred Korfmann's team found a ditch and a lower town outside, home to perhaps five to ten thousand people, but the historian Frank Kolb argued Troy was a princely seat, not a real city. Even Kolb called it the centre of its region: the quarrel is over the size of the town.

Was Troy the seat of power of its region, whatever the size of its lower town? Verdict: Established.

films.title: Ugarit, Hattusa, Pylos: did one enemy burn the Bronze Age world?
films.hook: Did one enemy burn them all?
films.caption:
Ugarit's last king, Ammurapi, wrote that seven enemy ships had done much damage while his troops and ships were far away, and then the city's letters stop. Inland, the Hittite capital, Hattusa, burned, but it had been emptied first, with no sign of raiders from the sea. Greek palaces burned around 1200 BCE, yet on Cyprus, Kition was rebuilt grander than before.

Did one enemy burn the great cities of the Bronze Age, from Greece to Syria? Verdict: Ruled out.

films.title: Wilusa in the Hittite archives: is there a record of the Trojan War?
films.hook: A Trojan War in Hittite letters?
films.caption:
The archives of Hattusa, the Hittite capital, name a kingdom in the far west, Wilusa, and Homer's Ilios was once Wilios. Around 1250 BCE a Hittite king wrote to the king of Ahhiyawa, most likely the Mycenaean Greeks, that they had been hostile over Wilusa and made peace. Hostile could mean angry letters, or war, and no Hittite text yet found says that Greeks attacked Wilusa.

Do Hittite letters about Wilusa, a name that echoes Homer's Ilios, record a Greek war against it? Verdict: Open question.

films.title: Tree rings and grain letters: drought and hunger at the end of the Bronze Age
films.hook: Did the weather turn on them?
films.caption:
Pollen in lake mud from Cyprus, the Syrian coast and the Sea of Galilee shows a long dry spell from around 1200 BCE, and juniper timbers from Gordion record three drought years in a row as the Hittite empire was ending. Letters of the time ask for grain and report severe hunger. Earthquakes are less clear: a 2018 study found a destructive quake at Tiryns and Midea unlikely.

Did drought and hunger strike the Bronze Age kingdoms as they fell? Verdict: Strong evidence.

films.title: A helmet of boars' tusks: how much Bronze Age memory is in the Iliad?
films.caption:
The Iliad was composed around 700 BCE, almost five hundred years after Troy Seven A burned, but singers recorded in the 1930s show that a tradition without writing can carry old pieces far. It keeps a Bronze Age helmet of boars' tusks, yet its heroes prize iron and the Hittites never appear. It is a chest of heirlooms, some Bronze Age, others added on the way.

Is the Iliad, composed almost five hundred years after Troy burned, a record of a real war? Verdict: Open question.

films.title: A perfect storm? The systems collapse idea for the end of the Bronze Age
films.hook: One cause, or a perfect storm?
films.caption:
Bronze needs copper and tin, almost no kingdom had both, and ships like the one wrecked at Uluburun carried them. Add trouble within, from a Cyprus official blaming Ugarit's own people to a strike by Egypt's tomb builders, and many historians see a systems collapse. But a storm of everything can explain almost anything, and each place fell, or didn't, in its own way.

Did many failures at once, from drought to broken trade and revolt, bring the Bronze Age world down? Verdict: Plausible.

films.title: Troy burned around 1180 BCE. Was it Homer's war, or a world coming apart?
films.caption:
Around 1180 BCE, Troy Seven A burned, leaving bronze arrowheads, unburied dead in the streets and heaps of sling stones nobody gathered up. The date later Greek scholars settled on, 1184 BCE, lands right beside the fire. But in the same decades the Hittite capital, Ugarit and Pylos burned too, tree rings record a savage drought, and the ground does not say who lit the fire.

Was Troy destroyed around the time Greek tradition places the Trojan War? Verdict: Strong evidence.

films.title: How the Library of Alexandria was filled: books taken from the ships
films.hook: How do you fill a whole library?
films.caption:
Around 300 BCE, Egypt's Greek kings, the Ptolemies, founded the Mouseion in Alexandria, with a library meant to hold every book worth having. Books on any ship that docked were copied and the library kept the originals, as the third Ptolemy did with Athens' copies of its great playwrights. Callimachus listed its writers in his Tables, now known only from scattered quotations.

Was the Ptolemies' library, meant to hold every book worth having, lost in one great fire? Verdict: Ruled out.

films.title: Brain warfare: how the fear of brainwashing led the CIA to MKUltra in 1953
films.caption:
In 1950 a journalist wrote of brainwashing in communist China, and in the Korean War captured American airmen signed confessions the United States called false. In April 1953 the CIA's head, Allen Dulles, warned of brain warfare, and three days later authorised MKUltra, with LSD as its star. Its records show who was paid, often through fronts, and only roughly why.

Did MKUltra, born of the fear of brainwashing, ever find a way to control minds? Verdict: Awaiting evidence.

films.title: Did Julius Caesar burn the Library of Alexandria in 48 BCE?
films.caption:
In 48 BCE, trapped in Alexandria, Julius Caesar burned the ships in the harbour. He mentions no books, later writers' figures grow with time, and Cassius Dio says warehouses of grain and books by the docks burned. Yet a generation later Strabo described the Museum at work, and more than a century after the fire Domitian sent scribes to Alexandria to copy its books.

Did Julius Caesar's fire in 48 BCE destroy the Library of Alexandria? Verdict: Ruled out.

films.title: MKUltra's safe houses: LSD slipped into the drinks of people who never knew
films.caption:
In New York and San Francisco, the CIA paid for safe houses where a narcotics agent, George White, slipped LSD into the drinks of people who had no idea, and some were ill for hours, or days. In 1963, the CIA's own Inspector General warned this put citizens' rights in jeopardy. Gottlieb later guessed about forty tests, and the records that could check him no longer exist.

Did the CIA secretly test LSD on people who did not know they had been drugged? Verdict: Established.

films.title: A purge, damp papyrus and war: the slow decline of Alexandria's library
films.hook: A library lost without a fire?
films.caption:
In 145 BCE, Ptolemy the Eighth turned on Alexandria's scholars, and the head of the library, Aristarchus, fled to Cyprus. Papyrus might last a century, sometimes two or three, so in damp Alexandria a book survived only if someone copied it. In the 270s CE, war wrecked the royal district where the Museum stood, and no writer describes the palace library at work again.

Did the library fade slowly, through a purge of its scholars, decaying papyrus and war? Verdict: Strong evidence.

films.title: How did Frank Olson die? The scientist given LSD without warning in 1953
films.caption:
In November 1953, at a retreat by Deep Creek Lake in Maryland, Gottlieb's team put LSD in a bottle of liqueur, and Frank Olson, a scientist at the Army's Camp Detrick, drank it without warning. Nine days later he fell to his death from a tenth-floor window, recorded as suicide. After his body was exhumed in 1994, the cause was changed to unknown, and two accounts remain.

How did Frank Olson die, nine days after Gottlieb's team gave him LSD without warning? Verdict: Open question.

films.title: Alexandria's books in four thousand bathhouses? The 642 story, checked
films.caption:
Alexandria's second library stood in the Serapeum, a temple torn down in 391 CE, yet no account of its fall mentions books. In 415 a mob murdered the philosopher Hypatia, but no ancient source ties her death to the library. The tale that the city's books fed four thousand bathhouses after the 642 conquest first appears in writing about five hundred and sixty years later.

Were Alexandria's books burned in 642 to heat four thousand bathhouses for six months? Verdict: Ruled out.

films.title: The CIA destroyed the MKUltra files in 1973. Seven boxes of receipts survived
films.hook: What was in the seven boxes?
films.caption:
In January 1973 Sidney Gottlieb, with the approval of CIA director Richard Helms, had a hundred and fifty-two MKUltra files destroyed. But the money was filed elsewhere, and in 1977 a CIA employee, seeking files a writer had requested, found seven boxes of vouchers and accounts. Like bank statements after the diaries are burned, they follow the money, not the thinking.

Do the seven boxes that survived tell the whole story of MKUltra? Verdict: Ruled out.

films.title: MKUltra in Montreal: the CIA money that helped pay for depatterning
films.caption:
In Montreal, the psychiatrist Ewen Cameron tried to wipe away mental illness with depatterning: weeks of drugged sleep, repeated electroshocks and recorded messages on a loop, and many patients lost years of memory. The CIA helped pay through a front from 1957, though Canada's government gave several times more. In 2025 a Quebec court let former patients bring a class action.

Did the CIA secretly help pay for Ewen Cameron's depatterning of patients in Montreal? Verdict: Established.

films.title: Clovis first? The spear points that built a wall of dates
films.caption:
In the 1930s, near a railway town in New Mexico, diggers found fluted stone spear points beside mammoth bones, and carbon dating put them at about thirteen thousand years old. A neat story formed: big-game hunters crossed from Asia through Beringia and walked south when the ice parted. Claims of older sites kept failing strict tests, and older dates bounced off the wall.

Were the Clovis hunters of about thirteen thousand years ago the first people in the Americas? Verdict: Ruled out.

films.title: Britain after Rome: the dark age where the legend puts King Arthur
films.hook: Why is it called a dark age?
films.caption:
Around 410, Rome's last armies left Britain, new Roman coins had stopped arriving in bulk, and almost nobody wrote anything down. Ancient genomes from early medieval graves in eastern England show up to three quarters of the ancestry came from across the North Sea, yet newcomers and Britons lie in the same cemeteries. This half-lit world is where the legend puts Arthur.

Was there a real Arthur in the half-lit Britain that Rome left behind? Verdict: Open question.

films.title: Older than Clovis: Oregon, Idaho, and a new challenge to Monte Verde
films.caption:
At Monte Verde in southern Chile, a peat bog sealed a camp with hut frames, mastodon meat and chewed seaweed, about fourteen and a half thousand years old, which experts accepted in 1997. Paisley Caves in Oregon and Cooper's Ferry in Idaho are older than Clovis too. In 2026 a new team argued its dates came from Ice Age wood washed in by the creek, and the jury is out again.

Were people in the Americas before Clovis, more than fourteen thousand years ago? Verdict: Established.

films.title: Gildas, the closest witness to the battle of Badon, never names Arthur
films.hook: Who won the battle of Badon?
films.caption:
Gildas, a British churchman, left the only account of the age by someone who lived through it. He tells of the siege of Mount Badon, a Saxon defeat fought in the year he was born, which points to a real battle within living memory. Yet he never says who led the Britons there, and an old Welsh poem that does name Arthur may have gained that line centuries later.

Was there a great British victory over the Saxons at Mount Badon? Verdict: Strong evidence.

films.title: White Sands footprints: seeds, pollen and quartz point to the Ice Age
films.caption:
In the bed of a vanished Ice Age lake at White Sands, New Mexico, researchers mapped sixty-one human footprints, mostly of teenagers and children. Seeds of a water plant dated them to about twenty-three to twenty-one thousand years ago, and when critics warned of old carbon in the water, pollen and quartz gave the same answer. Some experts still doubt the dates.

Do the White Sands footprints show people in the Americas about twenty-one thousand years ago? Verdict: Strong evidence.

films.title: Around 829, a Welsh book calls Arthur a leader of battles, not a king
films.caption:
The first firm date for Arthur comes around 829, in a Welsh book, the History of the Britons, about three hundred years after the battle of Badon. It calls him a leader of battles, not a king, credits him with nine hundred and sixty men felled in one charge, and already mixes him with folklore. The further we get from Badon, the more we learn about Arthur.

Was the leader of battles named in the History of the Britons a real man? Verdict: Open question.

films.title: Down the coast or through the ice? How the first Americans may have come
films.hook: A kelp highway to the Americas?
films.caption:
Twenty-two thousand years ago, ice covered almost all of Canada, yet the White Sands walkers were already south of it. The inland gap didn't fully reopen until about thirteen thousand eight hundred years ago, but islands off Alaska were ice-free by about seventeen thousand years ago, with food-rich kelp forests along the coast. Any camps on that old shore now lie underwater.

Did the first Americans come down the coast, rather than through the ice-free corridor? Verdict: Plausible.

films.caption:
Around 1136, Geoffrey of Monmouth made Arthur a king, conceived at Tintagel and carried away to Avalon, in a medieval bestseller. Seven years after fire destroyed Glastonbury Abbey, its monks announced they had found Arthur, with a cross whose words echo Geoffrey's story, not the 500s. Most historians see the find as a publicity stunt, made just when the abbey needed it most.

Did the monks of Glastonbury Abbey find the grave of King Arthur? Verdict: Ruled out.

films.caption:
Ancient genomes suggest the ancestors of Native Americans paused in Beringia, cut off by the ice, until their branches parted around twenty thousand years ago. Yet the White Sands footprints are as old as that parting, or older. Either the genetic clocks need adjusting, or the first walkers left few or no descendants, or, say the sceptics, the footprint dates are wrong.

Were people in the Americas by twenty-one thousand years ago, as early as the genes' first parting? Verdict: Strong evidence.

films.title: Was Cadbury Castle really Camelot? What the digs there and at Tintagel found
films.caption:
From around 470, someone powerful refortified Cadbury Castle, a Somerset hill that locals called Camelot by 1542, and raised a great timber hall there. Tintagel has given more Mediterranean pottery than any other site in Britain, and a slate scratched with a different name, Artognou. Powerful people lived in both places, but none of them left us the name Arthur.

Was Cadbury Castle Camelot, or Tintagel the place where Arthur was born? Verdict: Awaiting evidence.

films.caption:
Around the year one thousand, the sagas say, Leif Eriksson sailed west from Greenland to a land they call Vinland, where Norse settlers traded with its people, then fought them. But the sagas were written down about two centuries later, and they disagree on the details. For nine centuries, the story was all there was: no one had found a single Norse house beyond Greenland.

films.title: Homer knew King Minos of Knossos, but never mentioned the Minotaur
films.hook: How old is the Minotaur myth?
films.caption:
In the Greek myth, King Minos kept the Minotaur, half man, half bull, in a maze built by Daedalus, until Theseus killed it and followed Ariadne's thread back out. Yet Homer knows Minos of Knossos and never mentions a maze or a monster, and our fullest tellings come more than fourteen centuries after the palace's last great fire. Does the story remember anything real?

Does the Greek myth of Minos remember a real palace, a bull cult and a sea power? Verdict: Plausible.

In 1960, a local man led the explorer Helge Ingstad to grassy bumps at L'Anse aux Meadows, in Newfoundland. Eight years of digs, led by the archaeologist Anne Stine Ingstad, uncovered eight sod buildings, a bronze cloak pin, a smithy and broken iron nails from ship repairs. No shelters for animals: not a farm, but a base for mending ships and exploring.

films.title: Knossos: the palace Arthur Evans found, and the parts he rebuilt in concrete
films.hook: A palace built like a maze?
films.caption:
In 1900, Arthur Evans began digging at Knossos, on Crete, and within months uncovered a maze of corridors, staircases, light wells and storerooms around a central court. He believed he had found the palace of Minos. But much of what visitors see is his reconstruction in reinforced concrete, which critics say set his guesses in stone and admirers say made the ruins readable.

Did a great palace stand at Knossos, right where the myth puts King Minos? Verdict: Established.

films.hook: How do we know the year was 1021?
films.caption:
Radiocarbon gives only a rough date, but in 993 a burst of particles, most likely from the Sun, left extra radiocarbon in that year's ring in every growing tree. Three pieces of Norse wood from L'Anse aux Meadows, cut with metal blades, show that spike twenty-eight rings from the bark: 1021. The researchers call it the first known moment when humans had circled the globe.

Were the Norse cutting trees in Newfoundland in the year 1021? Verdict: Established.

films.hook: Why so many bulls at Knossos?
films.caption:
At Knossos, bulls are everywhere: a painting of young people vaulting a charging bull, stone vessels carved as bulls' heads, stone horns on the rooftops. Whatever the myth made of it, the bull sits at the heart of the palace's art.

Among the wood chips at the Norse camp in Newfoundland lay three butternuts and butternut wood cut with a metal knife. Butternuts don't grow there: the nearest grow almost nine hundred kilometres away, in New Brunswick, on shores where wild grapes grow too. So was Vinland a whole region around the Gulf of Saint Lawrence, and did the Norse stay for years or a century?

Crete's Linear A is still unread, but in 1952 Michael Ventris, building on Alice Kober's work, cracked Linear B: Greek, used for the palace's accounts at Knossos. One list, on the usual reading, sends honey to all the gods and the same again to the Mistress of the Labyrinth. So the word was written at Knossos centuries before Homer; what it named, the tablet doesn't say.

films.title: The Vinland Map and the Kensington Runestone: why both are ruled out
films.hook: Which Viking finds don't hold up?
films.caption:
In 1965, Yale unveiled a map said to be from the fifteenth century, with Vinland on it, but its ink holds a titanium pigment first made in the 1920s. The Kensington Runestone, reported tangled in tree roots, tells of Swedes and Norwegians in 1362, yet its language reads like Swedish of the 1800s. A possible Norse site at Point Rosee, dug again, showed no Norse presence.

films.title: The Thera eruption and the long end of the palace of Knossos
films.caption:
A little over a hundred kilometres north of Crete, the volcano of Thera exploded in one of the largest eruptions in human history. Yet Knossos carried on for generations, through fires and Greek-speaking masters, to a last great fire whose date is still debated. Long after, the Greek city of Knossos stamped a labyrinth on its coins: how far had the memory travelled?

His Book of the Sea guided sailors round the whole Mediterranean, coast by coast, marking harbours, fresh water and hidden rocks, and more than forty copies survive. films.caption:

In 1980 the geologist Thomas Aigner found that most of the temple's 173 big blocks carry the same yellow band that crosses the lion's chest. The Sphinx is what the quarrymen left standing.

Was the Sphinx carved from the bedrock, with its quarried stone used to build the temple in front? Verdict: Established.

Since 1978 teams have scanned beneath it with radar and sound, and where drills went down, cameras found only natural rock and cracks. Whether any crossed the hollow picked up in 1991, no report says.

From 1752 it gave up hundreds of black lumps, taken for burnt logs until one broke open with writing inside: rolls of papyrus turned to charcoal, so brittle a touch made them ash. A student trained a model on a faint crackle of ink spotted by a contestant, and the first word read inside a closed scroll appeared: porphyras, purple, also found there with a different method. films.title: Sponge divers, a wreck full of statues and a bronze lump with a gear inside
films.hook: What was inside the bronze lump?
films.caption:
In 1900 sponge divers sheltering from a storm off the small island of Antikythera found a wreck heaped with bronze and marble statues. Among the lumps of corroded bronze and wood raised with them, one split open as it dried in 1902: inside were a gear wheel and tiny Greek letters. For half a century, nobody could say for sure what kind of machine it was.

Was the corroded lump raised from the Antikythera wreck a Greek calculator of the sky? Verdict: Established.

films.title: Counting 127 teeth: how X-rays tied the Antikythera gears to the Moon
films.caption:
The historian of science Derek de Solla Price called the Antikythera fragments an ancient Greek computer, and in 1971 he X-rayed them and counted the teeth. One wheel had 127: doubled, 254, the number of times the Moon goes round the sky in nineteen years. Sharper pictures later fixed his mistakes, and each new way of seeing found more gears.

Were the Antikythera gears cut to follow the Moon's cycles across the sky? Verdict: Established.

films.title: Eclipses, a calendar and the Olympics: what the Antikythera gears tracked
films.caption:
In 2005 an eight-tonne X-ray scanner was brought to the Antikythera fragments in Athens. Turned by hand, the gears drive pointers for the Sun, the Moon and the date, a pin in a slot copying the Moon's uneven pace, while back dials count a nineteen-year calendar, an eclipse cycle and the games. It is the sky as the Greeks read it, in a box about the size of a shoebox.

Was the Antikythera mechanism a calculator of the sky, with gears for eclipses, calendars and games? Verdict: Established.

films.caption:
Texts on the Antikythera mechanism name all five planets the Greeks knew, each with a pointer and a little sphere, but the gears that moved them are gone. In 2021 a team used two cycles read on the front cover to design sixty-nine gears, more than half of them inferred. The planets are the boldest part of every reconstruction, and the part with the fewest surviving gears.

Did the Antikythera mechanism display the five planets the Greeks knew? Verdict: Strong evidence.

Ancient astronaut books and television shows call the Antikythera mechanism an out-of-place artefact, perhaps a gift from visitors; true, nothing this complex survives again for over a thousand years. But it carries Greek words, a Corinthian calendar, Greek games and Greek astronomy, limits and all. Most ancient bronzes were melted down; this one survived because it sank.

films.caption:
Stonehenge began around 3000 BCE as a ring-shaped ditch and bank, dated by the red deer antler picks its diggers left on the floor. The great ring of sarsens and the trilithons came around 2500 BCE, and the bluestones were rearranged until about 1600 BCE. Not one Stonehenge, then, but many, over some fourteen centuries.

Was Stonehenge built in stages by Neolithic farmers, from about 3000 to 1600 BCE? Verdict: Established.

films.caption:

Burned stumps point to people clearing land with fire, and nearly every palm nut found was gnawed by the Polynesian rat. Who did more is still argued.

Two great towns appeared, ringed by moats and ramparts, with a cone of earth twenty-two metres tall at Cotoca, and straight raised causeways, canals and reservoirs. The towns faded around 1400, before any European arrived.

films.caption:
Around 2350 BCE, carvers covered the burial chamber of King Unas with the Pyramid Texts. They speak of Sah, the Egyptian name for Orion, linked with Osiris, and greet the king as a companion of Orion. Many Egyptologists think the Great Pyramid's shafts were a road for the king's spirit. But no text yet found matches the pyramids to the stars.

Do Egyptian texts tie the three Giza pyramids to the three stars of Orion's Belt? Verdict: Open question.

films.title: A finger bone from Denisova Cave and the DNA of a people nobody knew
films.hook: A people known from a fingertip?
films.caption:
In 2008 a chip of finger bone came out of Denisova Cave, in the Altai Mountains of Siberia. About seventy percent of its DNA was the girl's own, and by 2010 her genome revealed cousins of the Neanderthals, on a branch of their own: the Denisovans. A whole human group, known from its DNA before anyone had seen its face.

Were the Denisovans a distinct human group, known first from the DNA of one finger bone? Verdict: Established.

films.caption:

Screened by its collagen, it turned out to be human, and in 2018 its genome showed one copy Neanderthal and the other Denisovan. Her mother was a Neanderthal, her father a Denisovan. When these peoples met, they had children.

Did a girl from Denisova Cave have a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father? Verdict: Established.

films.title: Denisovan DNA in people today, from Papua New Guinea to the Tibetan Plateau
films.caption:
Millions of people alive today carry Denisovan DNA: four to six parts in a hundred in some people in Papua New Guinea, even more among the Ayta Magbukon of the Philippines, and a trace across mainland Asia. Most Tibetans carry a version of a gene that keeps their blood from thickening up high, traced in 2014 to the Denisovans or people very like them.

Do people alive today carry Denisovan DNA, including a gene that helps Tibetans live high up? Verdict: Established.

films.title: A jaw from a Tibetan cave: how proteins and DNA in the dirt found Denisovans
films.hook: Who lived on the roof of the world?
films.caption:
In 1980 a Buddhist monk found half of a human jaw in a cave 3,280 metres up on the Tibetan Plateau. No DNA survived, but in 2019 proteins from one of its teeth matched the Denisovans. Denisovan DNA later turned up in the cave's dirt, with the bones of what they butchered: blue sheep, wild yaks, woolly rhinos. They lived with thin air long before us.

Did Denisovans live high on the Tibetan Plateau, long before our own species arrived? Verdict: Strong evidence.

films.caption:

In 2025 a Beijing team recovered proteins and a trace of DNA that point to the Denisovans. Not everyone is convinced: one skull may not speak for a whole people.

Is the Harbin skull, nicknamed Dragon Man, the face of a Denisovan? Verdict: Strong evidence.

films.title: Were the Denisovans giants? Two leg bones from the Taiwan Strait, measured
films.caption:
Online, you often read that the Denisovans were giants, and their bones are big. Two leg bones from the Taiwan Strait, with a Denisovan protein marker, suggest people about one metre eighty and one metre ninety tall, in a 2026 study not yet peer reviewed. Tall, like a tall person today. And a big tooth tells you about chewing, not height.

Were the Denisovans giants, as you often read online? Verdict: Awaiting evidence.

Scans of vases, mostly in private collections, found some round to about a thousandth of an inch: a lathe's work, some said. Those have no find-spot, and in a 2025 study, vases with a known past looked handmade. The test: a vase from a sealed, dated tomb that measures like a lathe's work.

films.title: Petrie's core seven: was its spiral groove in granite cut by a machine?
films.hook: A spiral cut by a machine?
films.caption:
Core seven is a granite plug left by a tube drill, picked up at Giza by Flinders Petrie, a founder of careful archaeology in Egypt. Its groove sinks a tenth of an inch in one turn; Petrie judged loose sand couldn't cut it. The machinist Christopher Dunn put that at five hundred times a modern diamond drill's feed and proposed an ultrasonic drill. Could hand tools ever do that?

Does the spiral groove on core seven, a granite drill core from Giza, mark the track of a machine? Verdict: Awaiting evidence.

films.title: Wabar: the lost city of the Empty Quarter turned out to be meteorite craters
films.hook: Lost city, or a fallen star?
films.caption:
In 1932, the explorer Philby crossed Arabia's Empty Quarter looking for Wabar, a lost city, and found craters ringed with black glass. A falling iron meteorite had punched them into the sand, and sand grains, emptied like tiny batteries by its heat, date the impact to about three hundred years ago. A blast as big as Hiroshima's, with no bomb at all.

Were the Wabar craters in Arabia's Empty Quarter made by a falling iron meteorite a few centuries ago? Verdict: Established.

films.title: How soft copper can drill hard granite: sand, a bow and twenty hours at Aswan
films.caption:
Can soft copper drill hard granite? The experimental archaeologist Denys Stocks found the sand does the cutting: quartz is harder than granite's feldspar, and the copper just carries it round. At Aswan, three men spun a copper tube with a bow over dry sand; in twenty hours it sank six centimetres. Only the exact groove of one ancient core, core seven, hasn't been matched, yet.

Could Egypt's craftsmen cut hard stone like granite with copper, sand, stone borers and time? Verdict: Strong evidence.

films.title: Scotland's vitrified forts: can a timber fire melt stone? The 1937 test
films.hook: Can a wood fire melt stone?
films.caption:
On hilltops across Scotland, Iron Age forts have stone walls melted into glass; to some writers, only an atomic flash could do that. In 1937, Gordon Childe and Wallace Thorneycroft set fire to a short wall of stone rubble laced with timber, and its stones fused into glass. Why the forts burned (an attack, a ritual, or builders hardening their own walls) is still argued.

Were the stone walls of Scotland's vitrified forts melted into glass by burning timber? Verdict: Established.

films.caption:
In 1998 the engineer Christopher Dunn proposed that the Great Pyramid was a power plant, not a tomb. A machine leaves traces, so the idea can be checked: the salt he read as a chemical residue is rock salt from the limestone itself, and sealed rooms above the King's Chamber hold work gangs' marks and a king's name: Khufu. It was the good kind of idea: one that could be tested.

films.title: Oklo, Gabon: a natural nuclear reactor that ran about two billion years ago
films.caption:
In 1972, French engineers found some uranium ore from Oklo, in Gabon, already burned in a nuclear reactor about two billion years ago, when Earth had no animals, let alone engineers. Then, the share of easily split uranium was about five times higher, and when groundwater seeped in, the rock went critical by itself. A nuclear reaction signs its work, and the signature lasts.

Was Oklo, in Gabon, a natural nuclear reactor that ran by itself about two billion years ago? Verdict: Established.

films.title: Lake Mega-Chad and the monsoon: how Earth's orbit turned the Sahara green
films.caption:
In what is now Chad, a lake once spread as big as the Caspian Sea, and dried-up lake beds across the Sahara hold the bones of fish, hippos and crocodiles. A slow wobble in Earth's orbit made summer sun stronger, and the West African monsoon carried rain deep into the desert. Then plants and lakes joined in: green made more green. How much the plants added is still debated.

Was the green Sahara watered by the West African monsoon, paced by a slow wobble in Earth's orbit? Verdict: Established.

films.caption:
On Gozo, next to Malta, two temples stand side by side, their back wall still six metres high. The people of Gozo called the place Ġgantija, the giants' place, and told of a giantess, Sansuna, who carried the stones on her head. Around them, archaeologists found the villages and pottery of farmers whose ancestors had sailed from Sicily: a giant's work, by ordinary hands.

Were the giant temples of Malta and Gozo built by farmers whose ancestors had sailed from Sicily? Verdict: Established.

films.caption:
In 2000, Paul Sereno's team found about two hundred graves in Niger's Ténéré desert, beside a vanished lake. Kiffian fishers were buried there first; after a long dry spell came the Tenerians, who also kept cattle. In 2008 the team read the skulls as two peoples; a newer study of their teeth finds them hard to tell apart. Ancient DNA could settle it, if any survived the heat.

Were the Kiffian and the Tenerians, buried by the same lake at Gobero, one people or two? Verdict: Open question.

films.title: How radiocarbon and tree rings put Malta's temples before the Great Pyramid
films.caption:
For much of the twentieth century, Malta's temples were thought to be echoes of civilisations to the east. Then came radiocarbon, corrected by tree rings, and in 1973 Colin Renfrew spelled out what the new dates meant. As dated today, the temples began around 3600 BCE, about a thousand years before the Great Pyramid: not copies of the East, but the islanders' own invention.

Did Malta's temples begin around 3600 BCE, about a thousand years before the Great Pyramid? Verdict: Established.

films.title: Egypt's Cave of Swimmers: real swimmers, or the dead in a watery world below?
films.caption:
In 1933 the explorer Almásy found painted figures, arms and legs spread wide, in a rock shelter in Egypt's far south-west, where it almost never rains. He called it the Cave of Swimmers, and thought they showed a real lake from a wetter time. Others see the dead, afloat in a watery world, as in Egyptian texts from thousands of years later. The swimmers still aren't telling.

Do the Cave of Swimmers paintings show living people in a real lake, or the dead in a watery world? Verdict: Open question.

films.title: Do Malta's temples go back to the Ice Age? Graham Hancock's case, weighed
films.caption:
In the last Ice Age, dry land joined Malta to Sicily. The writer Graham Hancock asks whether the temples are that old: stone can't be radiocarbon dated, they seem to appear without a learning curve, and in 1999 divers reported a sunken temple. Under the temples lie only farmers' hearths and pottery, but surveys are now mapping the drowned land toward Sicily.

Could Malta's temples go back to the Ice Age, with more of them now under the sea? Verdict: Ruled out.

films.caption:
About seven thousand years ago, two women were laid to rest at Takarkori, a rock shelter in south-west Libya where herders kept cattle by lakes and grassland. Their DNA, read in 2025, traces most of their ancestry to a North African line nobody knew, which split off some fifty thousand years ago and then stayed apart. But two women from one shelter are not a whole people.

Did the two women laid to rest at Takarkori carry a North African lineage nobody knew? Verdict: Strong evidence.

films.caption:
In 1902, workmen cutting water tanks in Paola, Malta, broke into the Hypogeum: rooms, passages and stairs carved by hand into the rock on three levels. From around 4000 to 2500 BCE it was a resting place for some seven thousand people, where mourners left beads, pots and figures. Its doorways were carved like the temples above ground: the dead were given a temple of their own.

Was Malta's Hypogeum, carved into the rock, a resting place for the dead from around 4000 to 2500 BCE? Verdict: Established.

films.caption:
At Nabta Playa, in Egypt's southern desert, cattle herders set up a ring of stones at least eighteen centuries before the first Stonehenge. One sightline points to the midsummer sunrise, when the rains were due. Some see a star map of Orion, but its star dates fall about fifteen hundred years before the big stones went up. A place to watch the sun, and perhaps to ask for rain.

Did cattle herders at Nabta Playa set up their ring of stones to watch the sun? Verdict: Plausible.

Speak into the niche of the Oracle Room, in the Hypogeum, Malta's underground cemetery, and your voice fills the rooms around it. Claims grew of a brain-changing hundred and ten hertz, but in 2014 the music researcher Rupert Till found its strongest resonances lower, around forty and seventy-five hertz. The room does sing; whether it was carved to sing is still open.

films.title: Dust off Mauritania, trees at Lake Yoa: how fast did the green Sahara dry out?
films.hook: How fast did the rain stop?
films.caption:
The monsoon that had greened the Sahara retreated south. Off Mauritania, dust blown out to sea jumps about five and a half thousand years ago, within decades to centuries; at Lake Yoa in Chad, the trees thin out over thousands of years. As the rains failed, herders left for the highlands, the oases, the south and the Nile. New lake cores could time the end, place by place.

Did the green Sahara switch off overnight when the monsoon retreated south? Verdict: Mixed record.

films.title: Why did Malta's temple culture end? Pollen, soil and ancient DNA
films.caption:
Around 2350 BCE, after more than a thousand years, Malta's temple culture came to an end. Valley cores show hills losing their soil as the land turned drier, and ancient DNA from three of the temple people points to a small, isolated population. Soil, drought, isolation and perhaps disease all have their supporters; not one catastrophe, it seems, but a slow unravelling.

Why did Malta's temple culture come to an end around 2350 BCE, after more than a thousand years? Verdict: Open question.

films.title: Fire, ruin and a ban: the rise and fall of Carthage, Rome's great rival
films.caption:
Greek writers put the founding of Carthage around 814 BCE, and radiocarbon dates agree. It grew rich on the sea and became Rome's great rival. In 149 BCE Rome came back: after a siege of almost three years the city burned, about fifty thousand survivors were sold as slaves, and ten senators ordered that no one live there again. Fire, ruin and a ban, say the ancient writers.

Did Rome burn Carthage, raze it, and ban anyone from living there? Verdict: Established.

films.title: Did Rome sow Carthage with salt? Tracing a famous story back to its source
films.hook: Did Rome really salt the earth?
films.caption:
No ancient writer mentions salt at Carthage: not Polybius, who saw the fire, nor Appian, nor the Roman lawyer who records a plough drawn across the city. Historians have traced the story upstream, through a 1930 history and a pope's order of 1299, to a tale written down by al-Bakri some twelve hundred years after the fire. The salt was sprinkled on the story, not on the soil.

Did Rome sow the ruins of Carthage with salt, so that nothing would ever grow there again? Verdict: Ruled out.

films.title: Under Roman Carthage: the burned houses of 146 BCE, sealed like a time capsule
films.caption:
On the Byrsa hill, a French team uncovered houses under a thick layer of burnt debris from 146 BCE, sealed when Rome cut down the hilltop for its forum, right on top of the old city. In 122 BCE Rome voted to send six thousand settlers to farm the land, and it became one of the granaries that fed Rome. Not bad, for earth said to be sown with salt.

Does the ground of Carthage bear out the famous story of its end, the fire and the salted earth? Verdict: Mixed record.

films.title: Carthage's tophet: small urns, stone markers and vows to Baal Hammon and Tanit
films.caption:
At the tophet of Carthage, small urns hold the burned remains of babies and young children, and of lambs and young goats, under stones recording a vow fulfilled to Baal Hammon and Tanit. Greek and Roman writers, mostly outsiders and often enemies, said Carthage sacrificed its children, and children and animals were given the same rite. Yet the bones are read both ways.

Was Carthage's tophet a sanctuary where babies and young animals were burned and buried under vows? Verdict: Established.

films.title: Were children sacrificed at Carthage? Two bone studies, two opposite answers
films.hook: What can the bones tell us?
films.caption:
Two teams aged infant bones from the same urns at Carthage's tophet: Jeffrey Schwartz's found the pattern of natural deaths, most around birth, while Patricia Smith's found a peak at one to one and a half months, too sharp, they argue, for natural death. Many read the vows and texts as sacrifice, at least at times; others see a resting place for babies who died young.

Were the children of Carthage's tophet sacrificed? Verdict: Open question.

films.title: Kerkouane, the Punic town nobody rebuilt, and the lost alphabet of Dougga
films.caption:
Kerkouane, a Punic town left around 250 BCE and never rebuilt, keeps its streets, wells and baths. Ancient DNA shows most of its people had ancestry like that of Sicily and the Aegean, many had North African roots, and hardly any came from the Levant. At Dougga, a prince's tomb inscribed in two scripts gave the sounds of a lost alphabet; its language is still mostly silent.

Was Kerkouane, a Punic town on Cap Bon, left around 250 BCE and never rebuilt? Verdict: Strong evidence.

long.description:
Small footprints in the mud of a vanished lake in New Mexico, many of them made by teenagers and children in the depths of the last Ice Age. For much of the twentieth century, the textbooks said people reached the Americas only about 13,000 years ago. How did that wall of dates fall, and what still stands?

We follow the Clovis points, the long fight over Monte Verde in Chile and its new challenge in 2026, the caves of Oregon and a riverbank in Idaho, the White Sands footprints and the argument over their dates, the two roads past the ice, and what ancient genomes say about the ancestors of Native Americans. Verdict on people in the Americas by about 21,000 years ago: Strong evidence.

long.title: King Arthur: The Search for the Man
long.yt_title: Was King Arthur Real? What the Earliest Sources Say
long.hook: Was there ever a real King Arthur?
long.caption:
In 1191, the monks of Glastonbury Abbey said they had dug up a lead cross that read: here lies buried the renowned King Arthur, in the isle of Avalon. Was there ever a real King Arthur?

Verdict: Open question. Weigh it yourself: residualcontinuum.com
long.description:
In 1191, the monks of Glastonbury Abbey said they had dug up a lead cross that read: here lies buried the renowned King Arthur, in the isle of Avalon. Was there ever a real King Arthur?

We read the sources in the order they were written: Gildas, born in the year of the battle of Badon, who never names Arthur; the line "he was no Arthur" in the Welsh poem Y Gododdin; the History of the Britons of about 829, with its twelve battles; the Welsh Annals, with Badon and Camlann; then Geoffrey of Monmouth, who made Arthur a king, and the French poet who named Camelot. We weigh the Glastonbury grave, follow the digs at Cadbury Castle and Tintagel, meet the candidates from Riothamus to Artorius, and grade each piece of the legend. Verdict: Open question. A real war-leader may lie behind the name, but no source from his own lifetime names him.

long.title: Vinland: The Vikings Before Columbus
long.yt_title: Vikings in America: How a Solar Storm Gave Us the Year
long.hook: Did Vikings reach America before Columbus?
long.caption:
A thousand years ago, someone cut wood with a metal blade at the northern tip of Newfoundland, and a storm on the Sun, frozen in the tree rings, gives us the year: 1021. Did the Norse really reach America nearly five centuries before Columbus? And where was the land of grapes their sagas called Vinland?

Verdict: Established. Weigh it yourself: residualcontinuum.com
long.description:
A thousand years ago, someone cut wood with a metal blade at the northern tip of Newfoundland, and a storm on the Sun, frozen in the tree rings, gives us the year: 1021. Did the Norse really reach America nearly five centuries before Columbus? And where was the land of grapes their sagas called Vinland?

We read the two Vinland sagas and where they disagree; follow Helge Ingstad and Anne Stine Ingstad to the grassy bumps of L'Anse aux Meadows and the eight buildings beneath them; date the wood with the cosmic-ray signal of 993; follow three butternuts south to New Brunswick; ask, with care, who the people the sagas met really were; and test the claims that did not hold: the Vinland Map, the Kensington Runestone and Point Rosee. Verdict: Established for the Norse at L'Anse aux Meadows around 1021. The Vinland Map and the Kensington Runestone: Ruled out. Where Vinland was, and how long the Norse stayed: Open question.

long.title: Knossos: The Palace Behind the Myth
long.yt_title: Was the Minotaur's Labyrinth Real? The Palace of Knossos
long.hook: Was the Labyrinth a real place?
long.caption:
A palace wall on Crete painted with a young acrobat flying over a charging bull. A Greek myth of King Minos, a maze and a monster, half man and half bull. And a clay tablet from the same palace that sends honey to the Mistress of the Labyrinth. Was the Labyrinth a real place?

Verdict: Plausible. Weigh it yourself: residualcontinuum.com
long.description:
A palace wall on Crete painted with a young acrobat flying over a charging bull. A Greek myth of King Minos, a maze and a monster, half man and half bull. And a clay tablet from the same palace that sends honey to the Mistress of the Labyrinth. Was the Labyrinth a real place?

We read the myth and see how late it was written down; follow Minos Kalokairinos and Arthur Evans into the hill of Knossos, and sort what is Minoan from what is 1920s concrete; look at the bulls and the double axes, and the debated link between labrys and labyrinth; watch Michael Ventris read Linear B as Greek, and find the word labyrinth in the palace's own records; then set the eruption of Thera and the fall of the palaces against the story. Verdict: Plausible. The myth plausibly remembers a real palace, a bull cult and a sea power. Whether the palace itself was the Labyrinth is an Open question. A living Minotaur is Ruled out.

long.yt_title: The US Paid Psychic Spies for 23 Years. Did It Work?
long.hook: Can a mind see across the world?
long.caption:
In the summer of 1974 a former police commissioner at the Stanford Research Institute in California drew a giant crane he had never seen, at a secret Soviet site about 10,000 km away. CIA analysts judged the crane accurate. From 1972 to 1995, the United States government paid for remote viewing: describing distant targets by the mind alone.

Verdict: Ruled out. Weigh it yourself: residualcontinuum.com
long.description:
In the summer of 1974 a former police commissioner at the Stanford Research Institute in California drew a giant crane he had never seen, at a secret Soviet site about 10,000 km away. CIA analysts judged the crane accurate. From 1972 to 1995, the United States government paid for remote viewing: describing distant targets by the mind alone.

We follow what the declassified files show: the Cold War fear of Soviet psychic research, the CIA's first money for Russell Targ and Harold Puthoff's work with Ingo Swann and Pat Price, the Army unit at Fort Meade and its code names, how a session worked and why judging a hit is so hard (the clues David Marks and Richard Kammann found in the transcripts, and the matches that felt uncanny but were wrong), and the 1995 review for the CIA in which Jessica Utts and Ray Hyman disagreed about the lab statistics while the operational record was found to be of no use. Verdict on remote viewing as reliable intelligence: Ruled out. The programme itself: Established. A psychic effect in the lab: Awaiting evidence.

long.description:
In 1929, in the library of Topkapı Palace in Istanbul, a piece of a world map turned up: drawn on gazelle skin in 1513 by the Ottoman admiral Piri Reis. Along its bottom edge, a coast runs east below South America. Is it Antarctica, mapped before the ice?

We meet Piri Reis and his Book of the Sea; read the notes in which he names his sources, about twenty charts and a lost map by Columbus; follow the Antarctica claim from a 1956 radio panel and a 1960 Air Force letter to Charles Hapgood's book; see why the coast bends; and look beneath the real ice of Queen Maud Land. Verdict: Ruled out for an ice-free Antarctica on the map. Strong evidence that the map keeps part of a lost chart by Columbus.

long.title: The Temple Builders of Malta
long.yt_title: Older Than the Pyramids: Who Built Malta's Stone Temples?
long.hook: Who built this, and when?
long.caption:
At dawn on the equinox, the rising sun shines straight through the doorway of Mnajdra, a stone temple on Malta built some five thousand years ago. Malta's temples are older than the pyramids of Giza. Who built them, how do we know when, and why did they stop?

Verdict: Established. Weigh it yourself: residualcontinuum.com
long.description:
At dawn on the equinox, the rising sun shines straight through the doorway of Mnajdra, a stone temple on Malta built some five thousand years ago. Malta's temples are older than the pyramids of Giza. Who built them, how do we know when, and why did they stop?

We follow Ġgantija and the giantess Sansuna of Gozo's folklore, the radiocarbon revolution that re-dated the temples, the Ice Age and drowned-temple claims, the cart ruts, the hunter-gatherers who crossed to Malta 8,500 years ago, the Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum and the thousands laid to rest in it, the Oracle Room and what was really measured there, and the end of the temple culture. Verdict: Established, built by Malta's own farming people from about 3600 BCE. Ice Age temples and Ice Age cart ruts: Ruled out. A Hypogeum carved for its sound: Open question. 110 Hz brain effects and sound-pattern spirals: Awaiting evidence. Bronze Age newcomers who cremated their dead: Strong evidence. Why the temple culture ended: Open question.

long.title: Carthage: Salt and Ashes
long.yt_title: Did Rome Salt Carthage? And Were Its Children Sacrificed?
long.hook: Did Rome salt Carthage?
long.caption:
In 146 BCE Rome burned Carthage. Then, the story goes, it ploughed the ruins and sowed the earth with salt. Under the same city lie thousands of urns holding the ashes of babies, and Greek and Roman writers said Carthage sacrificed its children. What do the texts, the ground and the bones really show?

Verdict: Mixed record. Weigh it yourself: residualcontinuum.com
long.description:
In 146 BCE Rome burned Carthage. Then, the story goes, it ploughed the ruins and sowed the earth with salt. Under the same city lie thousands of urns holding the ashes of babies, and Greek and Roman writers said Carthage sacrificed its children. What do the texts, the ground and the bones really show?

From the founding of the New City (the legend of the ox hide, and a date that radiocarbon supports) to the last siege, we trace the salt upstream through Ridley's 1986 study, a papal letter of 1299 and an 11th-century tale recorded by al-Bakri, dig into the burned houses sealed under the Roman forum, read the vows on the tophet's stelae, weigh the two bone studies that reached opposite answers, and visit Kerkouane and the Dougga bilingual. Rome burned and razed the city: Established. Salted earth: Ruled out. Child sacrifice at the tophet: Open question. Overall: Mixed record.
